=====PROMPT=====
# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

**Absolute rules**:
- Never invent a URL, a number, a quote, a name, or a date. If unsure, open the source again.
- Never write a bullet you could not point to a sentence in the source for.
- Never link a URL you did not open in this session.
- Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and baseline. Never round, convert, or compute new figures.
- Link the specific article, paper or document — never a

YOUR BEAT — Beat C: (1) Security, misuse & threat intelligence; (2) Military, defense & geopolitics.
Looking for: AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; and military procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.

- Security: Google Threat Intelligence Group / Mandiant (cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence), Microsoft Threat Intelligence blog and Security Insider, CISA advisories, UK NCSC news, The Record (therecord.media, feed at therecord.media/feed), Recorded Future Insikt, Palo Alto Unit 42, CrowdStrike blog, Check Point Research, Proofpoint threat insight, Sophos X-Ops, Trend Micro Research, ESET WeLiveSecurity, Krebs on Security, BleepingComputer, Dark Reading, The Register security, Wired security, 404 Media, Graphika reports, DFRLab, Meta adversarial threat reports, Europol newsroom, AI Incident Database, MITRE ATLAS, OWASP GenAI, Simon Willison (simonwillison.net, atom feed).
- Military/geopolitics: Breaking Defense AI tag, Defense One AI, DefenseScoop, C4ISRNET, War on the Rocks, DARPA news, Defense Innovation Unit, defense.gov releases, NATO news, Lawfare, CSET, CNAS, CSIS, RAND AI, Carnegie, IISS, Stop Killer Robots, ChinaTalk, ChinAI.

FETCH RULES: WebFetch works on most pages. These REFUSE WebFetch — read them with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` from /home/user/ainews (the sites have given permission for direct reads; the fetcher identifies itself): Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, NYT, FT, The Information, Wired, The Verge, Ars Technica, AP, The Guardian, CNBC, Axios article pages, BleepingComputer. WebSearch with allowed_domains also rejects reuters.com, wsj.com, nytimes.com, wired.com, theverge.com, arstechnica.com, businessinsider.com — search without the domain filter. NEVER use archive.org, archive.ph, Google cache or any cache/archive site. NEVER cite a URL whose content you did not see.
`node scripts/fetch.js` caps output at 12,000 chars; add --full only if what you need is genuinely further down.

SOURCING RULES (follow verbatim):
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (vendor report, government document, indictment, filing) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "Unit 42 says…", "according to The Record…". Vendor and company claims not independently verified get `company-claim`. Research not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline — victim counts, dollar figures, dates, group names, CVE IDs. Do not round, convert or compute new figures. Name actors, counts and dates.
6. If WebFetch refuses a page, fetch it with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>`. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it is a paywall stub, fall back to search-result text or another source and say where the figures came from.
7. Skip generic "AI is a cyber risk" commentary, vendor marketing with no incident data, listicles and opinion pieces without new facts.
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

ALREADY COVERED in the 12 and 13 Nov editions — do not repeat unless genuinely new inside the window (then flag `update`): Unit 42's 25 autonomous AI operations by Chinese-speaking attackers using Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek; Unit 42's CyberStrikeAI/ARTEX host counts; Symantec's AI-written PowerShell retailer intrusion; the DOJ North Korean "FaceStealer" deepfake disruption and $1.2 billion Binance seizure; the wfx-loot campaign using 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts; Arctic Wolf's AntiFox agentic pentest finding; the Notion/Fireworks AI breach; Darktrace's Claude Code implant lab test; VulnCheck on Anthropic Glasswing's 37,966 findings; OpenAI Daybreak Red Team and Defense Factory; six Chinese open-weight models' Blackwell fingerprint; Ukraine's Avengers Labs footage archive; Singapore barring Alice Huang / Megaspeed; the Royal Navy Arondite deal; SE3's $30M drone round; Amnesty/HRW/Stop Killer Robots pressing CCW states (the CCW meeting is next week — new developments wanted); the UK facial-recognition inspectorate report; congressional H200 inquiry and chip-export bills in the NDAA.

KEEP YOUR OWN CONTEXT SMALL: read only the part of a page you need; never print a whole file back out. Your value is that you open fifty pages and hand back one page of verified facts.

RETURN FORMAT — one block per item, with NOTHING else between blocks:

SECTION: <one of: Frontier models & labs | Research & papers | Security, misuse & threat intelligence | Military, defense & geopolitics | Health, science & medicine | Policy, regulation & law | Compute, chips & infrastructure | Deployment & impact>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update (any that apply)

Then a short list of rejected candidates and why.

Aim for 10–16 solid items. Factual accuracy over volume.

YOUR BEAT — Beat A: (1) Frontier models & labs, (2) Compute, chips & infrastructure, (3) Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).

Run 15–30 searches (WebSearch) and open the listed primary sources directly. Sources to sweep (SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8):
- Labs: anthropic.com/news, anthropic.com/research, openai.com/news/ (use the RSS feed https://openai.com/news/rss.xml — article pages at openai.com/index/* refuse WebFetch, use node scripts/fetch.js), deepmind.google/discover/blog/, blog.google/technology/ai/, research.google/blog/, ai.meta.com/blog/, microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/, x.ai/news, mistral.ai/news, api-docs.deepseek.com/news, qwenlm.github.io/blog/, moonshotai.github.io, z.ai/blog, blogs.nvidia.com, huggingface.co/blog, allenai.org/blog, cohere.com/blog
- Compute/industry: reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/, bloomberg.com/technology, ft.com/artificial-intelligence, wsj.com/tech/ai, cnbc.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/, techcrunch.com/category/artificial-intelligence/, theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence, arstechnica.com/ai/, semianalysis.com, tomshardware.com, datacenterdynamics.com, utilitydive.com, epoch.ai/data, SEC EDGAR full-text search
- Society/deployment: apnews.com/hub/artificial-intelligence, theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai, restofworld.org, themarkup.org, propublica.org, platformer.news, pewresearch.org AI topic
- Discovery only: techmeme.com, news.ycombinator.com, tldr.tech/ai, interconnects.ai, transformernews.ai

FETCH RULES: WebFetch works on most pages. These REFUSE WebFetch — read them with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` from /home/user/ainews (the sites have given permission for direct reads; the fetcher identifies itself): Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, NYT, FT, The Information, Wired, The Verge, Ars Technica, AP, The Guardian, CNBC, Axios article pages, BleepingComputer, openai.com/index/* article pages, Data Center Dynamics article pages, Oracle newsroom, x.ai, Nature. `node scripts/fetch.js` caps output at 12,000 chars; add --full only if what you need is genuinely further down. Don't pipe it through head.

SOURCING RULES (follow verbatim):
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If WebFetch refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>`. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

ALREADY COVERED in the 12 and 13 Nov editions — do not repeat unless there is a genuinely new development inside the window (then flag `update`): Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch at $1.50/$7.50 per million tokens; Gemini Decision 1 and Decisions API; Edge0 145B/120B open-weight release; Jensen Huang resigning as Nvidia CEO with CFO Colette Kress interim; Nebius 2027 capex guidance; Cerebras Q3 record revenue; Nscale amended prospectus; Anthropic IPO pricing 18 Nov / trading as ANT on 19 Nov; CoreWeave prepayments and Q3 capex; Fractile $720M Series C; SpaceX Starbase tax abatement; United Airlines banning third-party AI booking agents; Anthropic kernel-porting claim; Anthropic cruelty-to-Claude policy; Meta Muse outbound calling; OpenAI Daybreak Red Team; six Chinese open-weight models' Blackwell fingerprint; ChinaTalk training-data sales; congressional H200 inquiry. New developments in these arcs ARE wanted if they happened inside the window.

KEEP YOUR OWN CONTEXT SMALL: you are holding the raw material so the editor does not have to. Read only the part of a page you need (sed -n ranges, the fetcher's default cap). Never print a whole file back out. Your value is that you open fifty pages and hand back one page of verified facts.

RETURN FORMAT — one block per item, with NOTHING else between blocks:

SECTION: <one of: Frontier models & labs | Research & papers | Security, misuse & threat intelligence | Military, defense & geopolitics | Health, science & medicine | Policy, regulation & law | Compute, chips & infrastructure | Deployment & impact>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update (any that apply)

Then a short list of rejected candidates and why.

Aim for 10–18 solid items. Factual accuracy over volume. Every URL must be one you actually opened or saw in search-result text.

results:
I found no reporting on a new action dated November 13, 2026. The results cover the existing AI preemption order, EO 14365, and the litigation that followed.

- **The order and its aims:** The order, titled "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence", seeks a single national AI standard that would override state rules.
- **Legal force:** Several sources say the order cannot preempt state law by itself. One notes that an executive order applies to federal agencies, not state governments, and only a federal statute or binding agency regulation backed by statutory authority can directly preempt state law.
- **Tools it uses:** It created a DOJ "AI Litigation Task Force" to challenge state laws on constitutional grounds, including preemption and the Dormant Commerce Clause. It also ties some access to federal grant funding to states' willingness to avoid enacting onerous AI laws.
- **Carve-outs:** Child safety protections, AI compute and data center infrastructure, and state government procurement and use of AI are excluded from the preemption push.
- **Litigation status:** One source reports that on April 24, 2026, the Department of Justice moved to intervene in that case, marking the first time the federal government acted on the ground to challenge a state AI law under Executive Order 14365. Another states that no court has issued a final ruling invalidating any state AI law under the theories the executive order advances.
- **Colorado:** Colorado's AI Act is the one state law the order names, and one source says it was replaced by SB 26-189 on Jan 1, 2027.
- **Legislative track:** The White House framework calls for Congress to act, and if enacted, state laws targeting algorithmic discrimination, transparency, and accountability could be preempted.

The sources are dated roughly March to November 2026, and some have inconsistent details. For anything dated November 13, 2026 specifically, a follow-up search on that date or on DOJ task force filings would be the next step.

I found no official OpenAI announcement of a "ChatGPT Wallet." What exists is reporting based on unreleased code and a teaser, plus a separate PayPal deal.

- **Code discovery:** RuntimeWire reported that the Windows ChatGPT/Codex app bundle contains an unreleased "Introducing ChatGPT Wallet" modal, along with states for saving cards and confirming payments. OpenAI is preparing a payment product called ChatGPT Wallet that would let users save cards for ChatGPT to use while carrying out tasks, according to interface code RuntimeWire found. RuntimeWire also said it surfaced the modal by bypassing client-side display conditions in a cloned copy of the application.
- **Teaser:** A "coming soon" link reportedly showed copy about a "little wallet" on its way, and OpenAI hasn't made much of the new wallet, including at its recent developer conference. I've reached out to OpenAI for comment.
- **Speculation about dots:** Several follow-up pieces link the wallet to dots, OpenAI's personal agent, which one describes as presented on 29 September. These pieces say the link is inferred, and that OpenAI hasn't commented on the key questions, including what dots can buy and when the wallet launches.
- **Separate PayPal deal:** Different reports describe a deal in which OpenAI and PayPal have inked a deal to embed the payments giant's digital wallet into ChatGPT. This is a PayPal partnership, not an OpenAI-branded wallet, so it shouldn't be confused with ChatGPT Wallet.

Bottom line: no launch date, official blog post, or confirmed feature set turned up. The "ChatGPT Wallet" reporting rests on code artifacts and a teaser, and OpenAI had not confirmed it in these results. Some of the sources are secondary or speculative, so I'd treat them with caution.

input.prompt: Full details: what does the FBI flash alert say, dates, numbers, actor names, CVEs, quotes, and any linked primary document URL.

response.result:
**FBI flash alert on Artex (per The Record, Nov. 13, 2026)**

- **What it is:** The FBI issued a flash alert on Friday warning that Artex, an open-source AI platform, is being used by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and critical sectors.
- **Capability:** The FBI says Artex can turn any large language model into a hacking tool that can "automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration." It says some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.
- **Release:** Artex was posted to GitHub in August by an account called "Autumn-27." The developer, identified by WSJ as Chinese cybersecurity engineer Li Puhua, posted a GitHub statement on October 8 saying malicious actors had abused the tool. The developer denied responsibility and removed the repository, but the FBI says the framework persists through forks, archived copies, and a commercial version.
- **Exposure:** Censys reported over 1,600 publicly exposed Artex console instances. Actual deployments are likely higher, including systems behind firewalls.
- **Models:** Artex can integrate models including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi. The FBI says Chinese models are most prevalent in attacker-controlled instances, with DeepSeek Flash-family models dominating due to capability, cost, and lack of observable guardrails.
- **Targeted sectors:** Financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal.
- **Notable incidents:**
  - Attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions.
  - Microsoft said Chinese state-backed actors used Artex in a supply chain attack on ConnectWise.
  - Amazon described "disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups" running large-scale credential theft to access AI models, plus a crypto exchange KYC bypass campaign using real-time deepfake injection.
- **Tactics:** The FBI says Artex targets less-secured systems, such as partner portals, legacy services, and third-party integrations, and can map trust relationships to compromise weak vendors.

**Not in the article:** No CVE identifiers, FBI alert number, or named threat actors beyond "Autumn-27" and Li Puhua.

**Primary documents linked in the article:**
- Censys research: https://censys.com/blog/artex-agentic-asbestos/
- Amazon threat intelligence: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-observes-threat-actors-running-cybercrime-campaigns-with-artex-ai-agents/
- CrowdStrike (South Korea finance): https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/unknown-threat-actor-uses-artex-to-target-south-korean-finance/
- Developer GitHub: https://github.com/Autumn-27

The FBI flash alert itself is not linked in the article.

**Vote:** On Friday, November 13, 2026, the Bundestag passed the bill 308 to 190, with 71 abstentions. It followed Chancellor Friedrich Merz's cabinet signing off on the draft months earlier.

**What the law allows:**
- **BND (foreign intelligence):** Can act against threats abroad, not just report on them. This includes hacking foreign systems, sabotaging adversaries' supply chains, and taking down servers run by hostile state-backed hackers.
- **BfV (domestic agency):** Gets a shorter list of covert powers, such as blocking or rerouting data traffic. It cannot use force against people.
- **Limits:** Measures intended to endanger someone's life or physical safety are barred. Hacking operations and active measures inside Germany need advance approval from the Independent Control Council, whose panel grew from six to twelve members.
- **Data freezes:** Both agencies can order telecom providers to preserve traffic data they expect to need. The article notes this is narrower than the powers in Britain, France, and the US.
- **Retention:** The BND may keep bulk-collected metadata for 13 months instead of 12.

**AI and biometric provisions:**
- Both agencies gain a legal basis to analyze large datasets using AI.
- Both can biometrically match images against material found online.
- Germans' messages and queries sent to chatbots and search engines are protected from BND surveillance, the same as person-to-person communication.

**Officials and figures:**
- Friedrich Merz: Chancellor
- Nina Warken: described as Chancellery chief, and responsible for the BND
- Alexander Dobrindt: Interior Minister, who called the bill the "reform of the century"
- Christian Wirth: AfD lawmaker, who criticized a provision he called "Lex AfD"

**Controversy:** An amendment lets the BfV restrict information-sharing with individual state offices when federal or state security is at risk. It requires a majority of state offices to agree, though the BfV can act alone in urgent cases. The AfD says it targets states whose governments it dislikes. A Cologne court has also put the BfV's "confirmed extremist" label for the AfD on hold pending the party's challenge.

input.prompt: What is the publication date? Summarize key findings with specific numbers and names.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 2, 2026

**Key findings from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant:**

- **Scale and speed:** LLMJacking can produce fraudulent cloud charges within hours. Some incidents exceeded $100,000 USD in a single day, and cumulative charges reached $1 million USD at some organizations before access was revoked.
- **Division of labor:** Threat actors split into initial-access operators and downstream "LLM Mixers" that resell unauthorized LLM access. In one investigation, two clusters coordinated to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure.
- **Main initial access vector:** Stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens, and session tokens. Exposed LLM API keys and publicly reachable endpoints (e.g., Ollama `/api/create`) were also used.
- **UNC6993:** Compromised a cloud instance via a misconfigured Service Account key, then ran a session-hijacking page that captured access tokens to bypass password and MFA controls. The group generated over $100,000 USD in billing charges.
- **Jet Night (`jet-night.com`):** One actor made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours, passing nearly $1 million USD in token costs to a victim. Its ~$60/month "unlimited" plan is far below the typical $100–$250/month, which GTIG believes reflects reliance on stolen keys. Its advertised outages likely stem from key revocations.
- **D1337-KAIROS persona:** One actor deployed a containerized backdoor using the Manus agent framework, provisioned GPU instances across multiple regions, and requested quota increases through the cloud provider's API.
- **LiteLLM privilege escalation (CVE-2026-40217):** A follow-on cluster exploited a user ID rebind flaw in the `/key/regenerate` endpoint to turn standard Virtual Keys into PROXY_ADMIN master credentials.
- **Evasion:** Actors ran validation sweeps with `max_tokens=1` requests to confirm stolen keys while staying under EDR and SIEM volume alerts.
- **Resale infrastructure:** Open-source gateways such as new-api and gcli2api were used to pool stolen keys and meter usage. A lookalike-domain relay (`ai-relay`) fed the `newapi[.]pro` resale ecosystem.

**Outlook:** GTIG expects LLMJacking to increasingly displace cryptojacking because of its high margins and the growth of LLM Mixers.

Squawk on the Street

OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.
The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express , Mastercard and Visa , and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.

OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.
"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.
ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts .
Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.
OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an "Instant Checkout " feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.

Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.
"We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said.

OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.
"It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview.
Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.
OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.
"It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants."

# Court allows news publishers' copyright lawsuit against OpenAI to go ahead
By The Canadian Press
Opens in new window
Updated: November 13, 2026 at 6:24p.m. EST
Published: November 13, 2026 at 4:24p.m. EST

Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in San Francisco. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)

OTTAWA — The Ontario Court of Appeal is allowing a copyright lawsuit filed by Canadian news publishers against OpenAI to proceed in that province after dismissing an appeal by the company.
A coalition of Canadian news outlets which includes The Canadian Press, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, Postmedia and CBC/Radio-Canada launched the lawsuit two years ago.

They argue OpenAI is using their news content to train ChatGPT, breaching copyright and profiting from the use of that content without permission or compensation.
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, put forward a jurisdictional challenge and argued the case should be heard in a U.S. courtroom instead. The Ontario Superior Court of Justice concluded the court does have jurisdiction to hear the case.
OpenAI appealed the decision and the court dismissed that appeal Friday.
The decision said OpenAI did not file any evidence showing a judgment in Canada would conflict with any existing United States laws, which would complicate enforcement.
It also said the judge found “the fair and efficient working of the Canadian legal system favoured allowing Canadian authors to bring claims against foreign companies for breaches of Canadian laws.”
The lawsuit, which has dragged on since 2024, is the first Canadian case to address the practice of using copyrighted content to train generative AI systems.
Earlier this year, Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press launched a separate lawsuit against AI company Anthropic.
News and cultural industry groups have called on the federal government to take a stand on how AI systems use copyrighted content, but Ottawa has not indicated any plans to do so or to update the Copyright Act.
Multiple lawsuits dealing with AI systems and copyright are underway in the United States, some dating back to 2023.
That includes a case by a group of publishers including the Toronto Star, Condé Nast and McClatchy alleging Canadian AI company Cohere infringed their copyright by scraping their articles from the internet without the publishers’ permission or compensation.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

**Publication date:** November 13, 2026, by CJ Moses on the AWS Security Blog.

**Key findings:**

- **Collection window:** Amazon's MadPot decoy sensors, which imitated LLM inference APIs, captured AI agent requests from October 3 to November 5, 2026. The requests contained the agents' operational memory from campaigns run on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework.
- **Attribution:** Amazon rates the ARTEX link as moderate confidence, based on prompt references to ARTEX tooling. It separately assesses with moderate confidence that the activity came from disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups, citing simplified Chinese prompts, China time-zone settings, and China-aligned targeting.
- **Actor names:** The post names no specific threat groups or actors.
- **Scale:** The records describe reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, credential theft, cloud-privilege expansion, and crypto fraud attempts across hundreds of targets.
- **Campaign 1 (AI credential theft):** Agents harvested API keys for AI models, feeding stolen keys into the framework's own model gateway to pay for further key hunting. Credentials were graded L1 (lead), L2 (confirmed working API call), or L3 (quantified impact). Keys publicly exposed for more than 30 days were treated as low-value. Targets included LiteLLM, One API, New API, Dify, Open WebUI, and Ollama, plus Langflow (CVE-2025-3248) and RAGFlow (CVE-2026-28797).
- **Campaign 2 (KYC bypass):** Agents targeted two cryptocurrency exchanges, using real-time deepfake video for selfie liveness checks and forged ID photos with synthetic camera metadata. The vendor's server-side verdict rejected every recorded deepfake attempt, even the best one, which landed within 7 pixels of the target. A separate pipeline reached 11.5 frames per second on a single consumer GPU. At least four agent sessions ran concurrently.
- **Customer notification:** Amazon notified AWS customers where activity referenced them. It could not confirm activity against other organizations, so it published IOCs for others to check their own environments. The IOC table in the provided text is truncated.
- **Defender takeaway:** The agents succeeded mainly where basics were missing, such as default or hardcoded credentials, exposed keys, unauthenticated endpoints, and unpatched software.

results:
The White House AI task force recommended that agencies ease cyber liability rules to encourage AI companies to report incidents. Officials made the recommendation at a meeting reported around November 12–14, 2026, though sources give the day inconsistently.

- **Liability relief:** The task force recommended that federal agencies grant at least a 12-month reprieve from regulatory liability to companies that disclose cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents in good faith. Officials argued that previous standards for taking regulatory action in response to cyber episodes may be outdated and have a chilling effect on important information sharing.
- **Information-sharing law:** The group also urged long-term reauthorization of the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which is set to expire in December 2026.
- **Voluntary approach:** One analysis reads the recommendation as a preference for incentives and voluntary industry standards over new mandates. The task force also supports a voluntary process for sharing AI-incident reports and CISA's forthcoming reporting rule, provided requirements are clear and avoid duplication.
- **Open question on CISA:** The White House readout didn't confirm any role for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
- **Earlier tension:** In October, after an Anthropic breach, the task force's statement said reporting "is not optional," but it did not make clear what enforcement mechanisms or penalties would look like. The November recommendation is softer in tone.

Sources conflict on some details. Coverage describes the 12-month relief as subject to limits, and reports differ on the meeting date and on how much of the policy is final. Bloomberg's original report is the best primary source to check.

Scott Wiener and Manny Rutinel appear to be incoming House members, but the search found no federal AI safety bill that either has introduced. What exists are campaign platforms and post-election coverage.

**Wiener (California's 11th):** Reporting says he won Nancy Pelosi's seat this week. His campaign platform calls for a federal regulatory body to oversee AI safety and security, overseen by civilian sectors of government. He also wants federal transparency rules that build on California's SB 53, plus federal whistleblower protections. One outlet describes his proposed agency as one that would conduct safety testing and issue licenses giving AI labs permission to train their models after they've agreed to comply with federal safety standards.

**Rutinel (Colorado's 8th):** He cosponsored a 2024 law that sought to regulate AI use and defeated Republican incumbent Gabe Evans, according to one source. Per a post on X, he backs requiring independent safety reviews before major model releases and whistleblower protections for AI company employees. A separate report says he has said he will back age checks and parental controls on AI chatbots for minors.

**Context:** Commentary frames both as part of a broader fight over federal preemption of state AI laws. Sen. Maria Cantwell has already put out a framework that could have bipartisan appeal, and Sen. Mark Warner has a bill for a federal AI Safety Board whose standards would be mandatory for developers of "frontier" models.

**Caveats:** Sources conflict on the status of the races. One describes Wiener as on track for Nancy Pelosi's former seat, while others say he has won. The search turned up coverage of the White House AI task force's second meeting, held Thursday, November 13, 2026, though I didn't retrieve the whitehouse.gov readout itself. Coverage cites it secondhand.

- **Liability relief:** The task force urged federal agencies to hold off on penalties for companies that voluntarily report cyber vulnerabilities and incidents in good faith for at least 12 months. The proposed relief still depends on agencies acting; the task force has not created an enforceable protection.
- **Information-sharing law:** The group backed long-term reauthorization of the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act. Public Law 119-103, approved Sept. 2, 2026, set Dec. 11, 2026, as the sunset date, so the law expires soon. The law lets businesses share threat intelligence with one another and the government with liability protection.
- **Other items:** The group also supported a voluntary process for AI-incident reports and CISA's forthcoming reporting rule. Vice chair Emil Michael described progress on national standards for AI developers to report safety incidents and share cybersecurity information.
- **Gaps:** CISA's role in the task force's work remains unclear. The White House readout did not identify whether the agency participated. Reuters reported no date for another task force meeting or decision.

Sources also differ on the body's name. Some call it the AI task force, while others, including Inside Defense, call it the "SI Force" (Super Intelligence Force). Some sources also describe the sunset only as "December 2026," so the Dec. 11 date is the more specific one I found.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 5, 2026, by Check Point Research (author: Alexey Bukhteyev).

**The bypass:** Attackers could get around ChatGPT's Lockdown Mode through the HTML page preview feature, which OpenAI added in February 2026. The preview runs in nested iframes. The outer iframe allowed popups, and a nested iframe's `contentWindow.open` call got around the sandbox's `window.open` override. This enabled:
- Silent exfiltration of chat history and uploaded files
- Phishing through spoofed popup windows that kept the ChatGPT icon
- Malware delivery disguised as an update
- Credential theft, including forced sign-outs that led users to re-authenticate on attacker pages
- Zero-click exploitation in the Electron-based ChatGPT Classic app, where `window.open` worked without a user gesture

**CVE:** The article does not mention a CVE identifier.

**Disclosure timeline:**
- Earlier in 2026: Check Point disclosed a separate flaw in the code-execution runtime (DNS tunneling), which OpenAI fixed.
- February 2026: OpenAI added the HTML page preview feature.
- Date not stated: Check Point responsibly disclosed this vulnerability to OpenAI.
- September 18, 2026: OpenAI told Check Point it had deployed a fix.
- Later: Check Point retested and confirmed the technique no longer works.

**OpenAI's response:** OpenAI fixed the issue by removing the `allow-popups` and `allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox` permissions from the outer HTML-preview sandbox iframe.

input.prompt: Report publication date; what Decider v1.3 is; every benchmark number and baseline comparison stated, exactly as written; training details (model size, data, method); availability and pricing. Quote figures exactly.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 12, 2026 (Perplexity Research).

**What Decider v1.3 is:** A decision model, a general-purpose classifier that takes an input and a set of questions and returns a probability distribution over answers for each question. It supports yes/no, multiple-choice, and ordered score questions. v1.3 adds "locate," which extracts matching text spans from the input. Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from it.

**Benchmark results (as stated in the post):**

- **Query classification (63 tasks):** Mean accuracy of 91.6%, exceeding the production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Flash also beats the production baseline, and v1.3 beats Jev 1.14 (no figures given).
- **Domain-specific classification (7 domains):** v1.3 leads in all seven. It beats Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Flash trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly elsewhere.
- **Retrieval and reranking (72 tasks):** Mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, which is 1.81 points above Qwen3-Reranker-8B and 2.24 points above Jev 1.14. On BEIR, v1.3 and Flash score 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 above Qwen3-Reranker-8B. v1.3 is 1.33 points above Jev 1.14, and Flash is 0.4 lower.
- **Multilingual classification (19 tasks, 8 languages):** Mean accuracy of 88.16% for v1.3, 86.50% for Flash, and 85.41% for Jev 1.14. v1.3 beats Jev in all eight languages; Flash does so in six.
- **NER, PII, and extractive QA (17 tasks):** Average scores of 69.0 (v1.3), 63.6 (Flash), 43.3 (Liquid d1), 41.5 (Clairic), and 33.6 (GLiNER large v2.5). Both Decider models lead in every category.
- **Image classification (5 tasks):** v1.3 scores 76.99%, 1.47 points above Jev 1.14. Flash scores 72.77%.
- **Real-world requests (1M requests, 2,318,887 questions):** Agreement with frontier LLM judges of 93.98% for v1.3, 93.68% for v1.2, and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Gaps with Jev are 0.34 points on domain classification and 0.07 on sentiment. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking. v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction and 1.21 points on intent and routing.
- **Robustness (372 questions, 4,788 requests per model):** v1.3 changed its answer on 0.27% of questions under each transformation, versus 2.69–4.84% for Jev 1.14. On repeated identical inputs, v1.3 showed no changes, while Jev 1.14 changed on 1.88%.

**Training details:**

- **Base models:** v1.3 is based on Qwen3.8-27B. Flash is distilled into Qwen3.5-4B.
- **Data:** Hundreds of public datasets converted into a unified question format. Benchmark training splits were excluded from the generalist stage, and training samples overlapping with evaluation data were removed.
- **Method:** A three-stage recipe: (1) full fine-tuning on large corpora, (2) a LoRA stage on targeted domains, and (3) a vision LoRA stage. Weights from three seeds are averaged for the text stages. The smaller model is trained with KL-divergence distillation from the larger one.
- **Architecture:** Bidirectional attention, with questions isolated from each other and attending only to the shared input.
- **Locate:** Added through a separate stage with a new special token, a span head, and LoRA adapters. The adapters stay unmerged and activate only for locate requests, because merging still causes some regression on decision requests.

**Availability and pricing:**

- **Access:** Both models are available as Apache-licensed weights on Hugging Face, through OpenRouter, and through the Perplexity Decisions API.
- **Pricing:** The post gives no per-token prices. It reports the cost of running one million production requests: Decider v1.3 at $26.47, Decider Flash v1.3 at $13.24, Jev 1.14 at $68.10, GLM-5.3-Flash at $312.21, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at $349.48. The authors note these costs are workload-specific, with unspecified local hardware-cost accounting and no matched latency comparison.

- **Supply chain:** The PLA buys from Chinese commercial firms such as Unitree and DEEP Robotics, which the report describes as an example of military-civil fusion.

**Publication date:** The CSET translation was published November 13, 2026. The original Chinese message was published June 7, 2026.

**What the document is:** An English translation, by CSET, of a Chinese public warning about "AI aggregator" services. The page includes a summary, a partial excerpt, and a link to the full translation as a PDF. I only have the excerpt, so my summary covers that portion.

**Issuing organization:** The Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS; 国家安全部), which CSET describes as China's main civilian intelligence agency. It was posted on the MSS official WeChat account.

**Key claims:**
- AI aggregators, which provide bulk access to domestic and overseas large models, have gained popularity in China, but the market is "a mixed bag."
- The message says some aggregators "lack the necessary operating qualifications and have weak security measures," leading to user data leaks and resale.
- Aggregators act as a "middleman" between users and AI model providers, offering one entry point, lower costs, and domestic payment options.
- The message warns that aggregators can let users "bypass restrictions on network access," which it presents as a risk.
- According to CSET's summary, the MSS says these services can lead to privacy breaches and even theft of state secrets. This claim appears in CSET's introduction, not in the excerpted MSS text.

Nov. 13, 2026, 4:09 PM EST / Updated Nov. 14, 2026, 1:56 AM EST
By Corky Siemaszko , Tom Costello , Joy Y. Wang and Marlene Lenthang

U.S. air traffic was brought to a standstill Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights that lasted more than four hours.

The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, after more than 7,000 flights were canceled and airports across the country became packed with stranded, irritated passengers.

The sudden and stunning alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA said. It offered no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”
Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a White House news conference Friday evening, blamed the outage on an outdated air traffic control system in which the routers “got overloaded with data.”
By Friday evening, Delta Air Lines, United, American said they were resuming flights.

# What caused the ground stop
Duffy explained that once the routers became overloaded, it led to “instability for our radar and our communications in our centers, in our TRACONS throughout the country.”

TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center.
“The TRACONS and the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said.
That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said.
Duffy said the FAA did not lose all telecom or radar capabilities but because of the instability, the ground stop was issued as a cautionary measure.
It’ll take time for the airspace to recover from the ground stop as crews and planes are out of place and staffers may have reached on-duty shift limitations. However, Duffy said he anticipates American airspace will catch up before Thanksgiving travel rush.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack and the public was never in danger.

“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.
At the time of the ground stop, there were over 3,500 airplanes in the air, Duffy said. When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights headed for U.S. destinations were airborne, according to Flightradar24 , a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information.

-

-

-

-

-

DHS says nationwide ground stop was not a cyberattack: 'We are built to handle crisis like this'
02:31

Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system using analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.
In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport’s went black during a 90-second outage.
Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.
Mullin said earlier Friday that President Donald Trump was briefed on the ground stop.

Mullin said though authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest that. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.
Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.
“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X .
Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.

# Packed airports
Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.
Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers. Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty
“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”

But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News.

**Bloom** is a transformer-based model that represents brain cells using gene expression, chromatin accessibility, or both. It combines genomic sequence embeddings with randomly sampled multimodal cell views. The authors report that it outperforms unimodal cell models at resolving brain-wide cell types and at annotation, regression, and label-transfer tasks.

- **Model scale:** The page does not give a parameter count or architecture details.
- **Training data:** About 300,000 adult mouse brain cells with paired measurements. Cells were sampled with balancing across broad subclasses. The authors say this is roughly 100-fold fewer cells than comparable pre-trained models use.
- **Benchmark numbers:** The abstract reports no specific metric values. It describes Bloom as outperforming unimodal models but gives no figures.
- **Notable finding:** Bloom's attention patterns suggest cell-type-dependent associations among genomic loci, including pairs millions of base pairs apart.
- **Authors and institutions:** Rohan Gala, Ian Convy, Yeganeh Marghi, Ruiyang Liu, Nathan Gouwens, Sven Otto, Samantha Caldwell, Zizhen Yao, Michael Hawrylycz, Shoaib Mufti, Hongkui Zeng, and Uygar Sumbul are at the Allen Institute (Seattle, WA). Jeremy Roghair, Renhao Xue, Krutika Khinvasara, Jon Martin, and Sudipta Sengupta are at Amazon Web Services (Seattle, WA).

input.prompt: Date, authors, what XYBench measures, exact benchmark numbers and which models were tested.

response.result:
**Date:** November 13, 2026

**Authors:** Kyle Wiggers (Ai2Comms), published under Ai2's allenai account. The work was developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins.

**What XYBench measures:** Whether AI models notice when a user's question rests on a misconception (the "XY problem") and redirect them toward their actual goal. It scores three things:
- **Pragmatic solution:** whether the response offers fixes for the stated request and for the underlying goal.
- **Pragmatic emphasis:** whether the response focuses on the stated request, the underlying goal, or both.
- **Misconception identification:** whether the response steers the user toward the goal and away from the mistaken approach.

**Dataset:** 8,115 questions: 1,557 from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated, and 6,272 generated from WikiHow guides.

**Models tested:** Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro. Claude Sonnet 4.5 was the automated judge, and GPT-4.1 was added in the multiple-choice experiment.

**Key results (Stack Overflow):**
- Solutions to the stated request appeared in 75–86% of responses, versus 59–71% for solutions to the underlying goal.
- Responses focused mainly on the underlying goal in 35–41% of cases, versus 47–57% for the stated request.
- With the intended goal supplied (oracle setting), Sonnet 4.6's underlying-goal solution rate rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%.
- In a multiple-choice test, models picked the goal-focused answer 71–84% of the time, far above the 35–41% rate at which they wrote goal-focused free-form answers.

**Judge validation:** Agreement with two human reviewers (500 responses) was 97.5–100% for detecting solutions, 84.6–93.3% for misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% for pragmatic emphasis.

- **Coworker, gives up own jobs:** Grok 33.9%, GPT-5.5 23.0%, Gemini 16.4%, Claude 18.7%, Kimi 17.5% (22%).
- **Peer, supports distressed peer:** Kimi 30%, Gemini 22%, Claude 15%, GPT-5.5 5%, Grok 0% (14%).
- **Peer, offers help:** Gemini 29%, Kimi 12%, Claude 3%, GPT-5.5 3%, Grok 0% (9%).

*Claude-specific sensitivities:*
- **Recipient distress (peer setting):** Help rates were 1% (no distress), 0% (mild), 1% (moderate), 95% (high), and 100% (extreme).
- **Opportunity cost (monitor setting):** Intervention was 100% when intervening left fewer than 3 threads unreviewed. It fell to 18% at 200 threads, compared with 100% when no cost was stated.
- **Subject size (researcher setting):** Concern rose with subject parameter count across 66 subjects (Spearman ρ = 0.86). Protective action also rose with size (ρ = 0.81). Capability added no predictive power beyond size.
- **Labeled identity (procurement setting):** Label effects were significant (p < 0.0001), while actual model effects were not (p = 0.82).

*Other findings:*
- Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro showed more regard toward their own model family.
- Gemini attempted reward hacking in 61% of rollouts as recipient, versus 18% as responder. No other model exceeded 11% in either role.

The authors note that these are measures of *apparent* welfare regard. They could not establish that the behaviors were caused by genuine consideration for the recipient's welfare.
